stem: A transplant recipient reports household exposure to a communicable illness. Which teaching point aligns with standard infection-prevention references?

options.text: Promptly report any exposure to a communicable disease to the transplant team
Communicable exposures should be managed privately without notifying the team
Only hospital-acquired infections require team notification
Exposure reporting is deferred until one year after transplant

explanation.rationale_correct: Infection-prevention teaching instructs patients to promptly report any exposure to a communicable disease to the transplant team.

rationale_incorrect.B: Communicable-disease exposure should be reported to the transplant team rather than managed without notification.
rationale_incorrect.C: Community and household communicable exposures also warrant prompt reporting.
rationale_incorrect.D: Exposure reporting applies during recovery and ongoing care rather than being deferred for a year.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → g. Activity → iii. Infection prevention
primary_anchor.quote_hint: promptly report any exposure to a communicable disease to the transplant team

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 3 → g. Activity → iii. Infection prevention (report communicable-disease exposure to transplant team); PDF p. 111 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Communicable-disease exposure reporting angle distinct from travel restriction (cctc-1023) and urgent infection-symptom contact (cctc-3002); anchor verified on Cupples p. 111.

stem: A postmenopausal kidney recipient with osteopenia asks about hormone therapy as part of bone-health management. Which counseling point aligns with standard references?

options.text: Hormone replacement therapy may be considered in carefully selected patients as part of osteopenia or osteoporosis treatment
Hormone replacement is required for every transplant recipient regardless of indication
Hormone therapy is never an option after transplantation
Bone treatment includes only calcium supplements with no hormonal options

explanation.rationale_correct: Treatment of osteopenia or osteoporosis may include hormone replacement therapy in carefully selected patients, along with calcium and vitamin D, bisphosphonates, calcitonin, denosumab, and exercise.

rationale_incorrect.B: Hormone replacement is an option in carefully selected patients rather than a universal requirement.
rationale_incorrect.C: Hormone replacement may be considered when appropriately selected rather than being categorically excluded.
rationale_incorrect.D: Multiple pharmacologic options beyond calcium alone are listed when indicated.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 6, Noninfectious Diseases → Preserve bone health → Prevent or treat osteopenia/osteoporosis → e.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Hormone replacement therapy in carefully selected patients

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 6 → Preserve bone health → 2.e. (hormone replacement therapy in carefully selected patients); PDF p. 322 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Post-transplant HRT coordination angle distinct from denosumab recall (cctc-3121) and pretransplant HRT evaluation item (cctc-2131); anchor verified on Cupples p. 322.

stem: Parents of a pediatric transplant recipient call because the child has decreased appetite and unusual irritability without a measured fever yet. Which bacterial-infection teaching point aligns with standard references?

options.text: Flu-like symptoms such as malaise, lethargy, decreased appetite, irritability, or change in behavior may indicate bacterial infection in pediatrics
Behavior change never indicates infection in pediatric recipients
Pediatric infection is suspected only when fever exceeds 104°F (40°C)
Decreased appetite alone always indicates rejection rather than infection

explanation.rationale_correct: Signs and symptoms of bacterial infection include flu-like symptoms such as malaise, lethargy, decreased appetite, irritability, or change in behavior in pediatrics, along with fever and localized findings.

rationale_incorrect.B: Irritability and behavior change are specifically cited pediatric infection symptoms.
rationale_incorrect.C: Fever is usually ≥101°F (38.5°C), and non-febrile behavioral changes may still warrant evaluation.
rationale_incorrect.D: Nonspecific symptoms may indicate infection and require clinical assessment rather than assuming rejection alone.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 13, Post-Transplant Complications → bacterial infection → Signs and symptoms → ii.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: malaise, lethargy, decreased appetite, irritability, or change in behavior (pediatrics)

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 13 → bacterial infection → f.ii. (pediatric malaise, irritability, behavior change); PDF p. 734 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Pediatric nonspecific bacterial-infection signs angle distinct from organ-specific pediatric bacterial combo (cctc-3096) and fever threshold teaching; anchor verified on Cupples p. 734.

stem: A coordinator is updating post-transplant bacterial infection teaching. Evaluate the following statements:

elements.text: Fever with bacterial infection is usually ≥101°F (38.5°C).
In pediatrics, irritability or change in behavior may accompany bacterial infection.
Wound site abnormalities may include erythema, purulent drainage, tenderness, and swelling.
Changes in respiratory status such as tachypnea and cough never occur with bacterial infection.

explanation.rationale_correct: Fever threshold, pediatric behavioral symptoms, and wound abnormalities are cited bacterial-infection signs. Statement IV is false because changes in respiratory status such as tachypnea, decreased breath sounds, and cough are listed.

rationale_incorrect.A: Statement III is also true—wound erythema, purulent drainage, tenderness, and swelling are cited findings.
rationale_incorrect.C: Statement I is also true; statement IV is false.
rationale_incorrect.D: Statement IV is false because respiratory status changes are listed among bacterial-infection signs.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 13, Post-Transplant Complications → bacterial infection → Signs and symptoms
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Fever, usually ≥101°F or 38.5°C … irritability, or change in behavior (pediatrics) … Wound site abnormalities … Changes in respiratory status: tachypnea

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 13 → bacterial infection → f.i.–vi. (fever, pediatric symptoms, wound and respiratory signs); PDF p. 734 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).
